HMW-V17: Vendor Job Search & Quick-Find

How might we let vendor operators quickly locate specific jobs in their list — by trip ID, customer, or MAWB — without breaking the dense-table design or adding a separate search page?
Context: The vendor app currently has no text search (DESIGN.md: "No search — no search input currently (future iteration)"). Vendors have status pills, service pills, and a date range filter — but no way to find a job by trip ID (e.g., "where is DO-007?"), customer name ("show all TikTok jobs"), or MAWB. At 5–30 jobs/day with 50-per-page pagination, history accumulates quickly. The admin app's filter bar has a single search input as its first element. The vendor filter bar should converge on the same pattern — but the vendor's narrower context (no vendor column, simpler query vocabulary) changes the design constraints.

Status Quo — No Search Gap

The current vendor filter bar has status pills + service pills + date range. Vendor must scroll through pages or use the date range to narrow results. No way to jump directly to a trip ID or a specific customer's jobs.

Option A: Inline Text Search Recommended

Compact · Real-time · No extra row
Add a compact search input to the existing filter bar's second row — left of the "Service" label. Same 4px radius, 1px border, 11px font as all other inputs. Searches Trip ID, Customer name, and MAWB in real time. Combines with existing segment + service + date filters. Clears via the × button. When the input has a value, it shows as active (dark border) so vendors know search is in effect.
Pros
· Matches admin app's filter bar pattern exactly
· Handles all query types (trip ID lookup, customer name, MAWB scan)
· No structural change — same 2-row filter bar
· Chainable with other filters (search "TikTok" + service "EC")
· Expected pattern — no onboarding needed
Cons
· Adds 200px of permanent width to the filter row
· At 768px viewport, filter row wraps — needs careful responsive treatment
· Free-text search has no autocomplete for trip IDs the vendor may not remember

Option B: Customer Quick-Filter Pills

Structural · Predictable · Limited scope
Add a third row to the filter bar: customer name pills derived from the vendor's actual job history. Clicking a customer pill filters the table to that customer's jobs. No freetext input — the customer set is always finite and known. Works well when vendors serve a small number of distinct customers (HaleSun serves TikTok, Shopee, and Shein; 3 pills is clean). Degrades if a vendor serves 10+ customers (too many pills, row wraps badly).
Pros
· Zero typing — tap once to filter by customer
· No ambiguity — pills are derived from actual job data
· Works well at 768px (pills wrap neatly)
· Chainable with service + date filters
· Obvious affordance — no placeholder text needed
Cons
· Cannot find a specific trip ID or MAWB (most urgent use case)
· Breaks for vendors with many customers (10+ pills = unusable)
· Adds a permanent third filter row — heavier visual weight
· Overlap with "All" status pill makes the pattern harder to read

Option C: Search with Smart Suggestions

Richest UX · Most build effort · Phase 2
A text input that shows autocomplete suggestions as the user types: customer names (from job history), trip IDs (exact match on DO-* prefix), and MAWB numbers. Selecting a suggestion snaps directly to that result. The dropdown is a floating card (4px radius, 1px border, subtle shadow — same as other popovers in the system). This is the most capable option but requires the most build effort and introduces a new interaction pattern (autocomplete) into a system that otherwise avoids them.
Pros
· Fastest for exact lookups — type 3 chars, see trip IDs
· Surfaces customers without requiring freetext recall
· Drop-down acts as a "recently-used" affordance
· Best for large job histories (200+ jobs across date ranges)
Cons
· Highest implementation cost
· Autocomplete adds interaction complexity for simple queries
· Dropdown management (open/close, keyboard nav) is a non-trivial UX surface
· Overengineered for the current scale (most vendors: <50 active jobs)

Verdict: Option A — Inline Text Search

Implement Option A. A compact search input in the existing filter row is the right call for this product phase.

  • Mirrors the admin app. Admin's filter bar leads with a single search input. Vendors using both apps will find the same pattern — zero relearning.
  • Covers all query types. Trip ID lookup ("DO-007"), customer name ("TikTok"), and MAWB scan are the three real search moments. A single input handles all three.
  • No structural change. The 2-row filter bar stays 2 rows. Service pills and date range remain in the same row. No new visual weight.
  • Chainable. Searching "TikTok" while the "EC" service pill is active gives "all TikTok customs-clearance jobs" — no extra design work needed.
  • Option B is a complement, not a replacement. Customer pills add value for vendors serving a small set of known customers (e.g., 3 customers). Ship it as a v1.1 enhancement on top of Option A if user research confirms the pattern — not instead of it.
  • Option C is a future concern. Autocomplete is correct for large datasets (500+ jobs). At the current scale (<50 active jobs per vendor), the suggestion overhead isn't warranted. Revisit at v2.

Responsive note: At 768px viewport, the filter row wraps. The search input should appear first in the wrapped layout (above service pills), so it remains the primary filter affordance on tablets. On ≥1024px, it sits left of the Service label in the same row.

Search scope: Trip ID (exact prefix match), Customer name (case-insensitive substring), MAWB (exact substring). Location names intentionally excluded — vendors know their locations by service and date, not by warehouse name.

Open questions for user input:
1. Highlight matches: Should the search term be highlighted in the table (as shown in the mockup with the faint blue highlight on matched text)? Or is a filtered result set sufficient without inline highlighting?
2. Scope of search: Should MAWB be searchable? Vendors operating at air cargo terminals may have the MAWB on a printout but not the Trip ID. Including MAWB makes the input more useful but increases the search logic complexity.
3. Customer pills as v1.1: Worth implementing Option B's customer pills as a secondary enhancement alongside Option A — or does the segment pill + search combination provide sufficient filtering for the current customer set?
